title: Glass Towers
objective: After this level you can explain the curtain walls of glass towers.
summary: A curtain wall is a nonbearing skin hung on the frame. Air conditioning and cheap postwar energy made glass towers practical; Lever House (1952) led in New York. Glass's catch: solar heat.

cards.headline: In 2013, a London skyscraper melted parts of a car.
cards.body: Sunlight bounced off the curved glass face of 20 Fenchurch Street, nicknamed the Walkie-Talkie, and was concentrated onto the street below, where it melted part of a parked Jaguar. So how did so many towers end up wrapped in glass?

cards.headline: A wall that hangs
cards.body: Level 8 split the jobs: the frame carries the floors, and the outer wall holds up only itself, hanging on the frame. That outer skin is called a curtain wall: a nonbearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to the building's structural frame. The name fits. Like a curtain, it hangs from something else and holds nothing up.

cards.headline: Glass needed cheap energy
cards.body: All-glass towers only became practical in the mid-20th century, with better air conditioning and cheap, plentiful energy. After World War II, low energy costs boosted the idea of the tower as a glass prism. In New York, Lever House (1952), designed by Gordon Bunshaft of SOM, was the first commercial building with a glass curtain wall, its glass held by extruded aluminum. It was widely copied.

cards.fact: Glass buildings have always had a heat problem.
cards.context: Even Level 8's Crystal Palace suffered: records show its indoor temperatures were extremely unstable, and it amplified peak summer heat. Glass lets the sun in, and a curved glass face can concentrate it too. After the Walkie-Talkie's glare, a permanent sunshade of horizontal aluminum fins was approved for the tower.

cards.headline: Glass towers: glazed
learned: A curtain wall is a nonbearing skin hung on the frame
Air conditioning and cheap energy made glass towers practical
Lever House (1952): New York's first glass curtain wall
Glass's catch: heat from the sun

questions.prompt: What is the curtain wall of a glass tower?

options.label: The inside walls that divide the offices
A thick wall that carries the floors above
options.rationale: That's a load-bearing wall; a curtain wall carries nothing but itself.

options.label: A nonbearing outer wall attached to the structural frame
A fabric screen hung inside the windows
options.rationale: The name is an analogy; it's glass, metal or masonry.

questions.explanation: A curtain wall is a nonbearing wall of glass, metal or masonry attached to the building's exterior structural frame.

questions.prompt: Why did all-glass office towers only become practical in the mid-20th century?

options.label: Glass was invented shortly before
options.rationale: Glass is far older; Level 8's Crystal Palace used it in 1851.

options.label: Better air conditioning and cheap energy arrived
Steel frames were first invented then
options.rationale: Steel frames date back to 1880s Chicago.

options.label: Cities began banning brick buildings
options.rationale: No ban; energy and cooling made the difference.

questions.explanation: Fully glazed towers needed air conditioning and cheap, abundant energy, which came in the mid-20th century.

questions.prompt: What problem do Level 8's Crystal Palace and London's Walkie-Talkie share?

options.label: Glass letting in, or concentrating, the sun's heat
Walls too heavy for their foundations
options.rationale: Glass walls are light; the problem was heat.

options.label: Frames that swayed badly in the wind
options.rationale: Wind isn't the shared problem here.

options.label: Parts too big to make in a factory
options.rationale: The Crystal Palace was built from factory-made parts.

questions.explanation: The Crystal Palace amplified summer heat; the Walkie-Talkie's curved glass concentrated sunlight enough to melt car parts.
